variants.name: System.Text.Json exclusion on the shared type
variants.implementation_notes: On .NET, the projection is usually declared on the type itself: mark members that must never reach the wire with [JsonIgnore], drop value-dependent fields with JsonIgnoreCondition.WhenWritingNull or WhenWritingDefault, and keep navigation properties and internal notes out of every payload; the serializer then emits only what is left. What replaces the classic filter object is the serializer's attribute contract plus one JsonSerializerOptions instance, so no per-message copying code exists. The classic explicit projection is still justified when a member is visible to one receiver and not another: a single [JsonIgnore] cannot express per-receiver views, so those cases move to a DTO (see the sibling variant) or to a custom converter.
pitfalls: DefaultIgnoreCondition is global to the options instance: turning it on for one payload also drops legitimate zero values (0, false, default enums) everywhere that options object is reused.
[JsonIgnore] is asymmetric in practice - it also blocks deserialization, so the same type can no longer be used to read back the full message.

Attribute-based exclusion lives in the domain model: serializing the entity directly from EF Core then pulls navigation properties the pattern was meant to remove - the documented cure is a projection, not another attribute.

variants.name: narrow DTO/record built with a LINQ projection
variants.idiom_name: Select into a record DTO instead of serializing the tracked entity
variants.implementation_notes: The alternative .NET realization builds a different type: project the source (entity, message object or query) into a narrow record or DTO and serialize that, which is also the documented way to stop EF Core navigation properties from blowing up a payload. What replaces the classic filter object is the DTO plus one Select/constructor call per seam, and the wire contract then exists as a type that can be contract-tested. It is the right choice when several receivers need different field sets from the same source (each gets its own DTO) and the shared type must not be annotated for serialization at all.
pitfalls: A DTO duplicated from the entity rots quietly: when the producer adds a field, the projection keeps compiling and the receiver silently misses the data - keep a contract test or a mapper generation step.

Select(...) into an unmapped type must stay server-translatable in EF Core; using a method the provider cannot translate silently switches to client evaluation (or throws) and the filter stops being a database projection.
Records project only what is listed, so a DTO that omits the message id or correlation fields breaks deduplication exactly like any other over-filtering.
